verses.text: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He didn’t do that which was right in Yahweh his God’s eyes, like David his father.
But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, yes, and made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom Yahweh cast out from before the children of Israel.
He sacrificed and burned incense in the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war. They besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.
At that time Rezin king of Syria recovered Elath to Syria, and drove the Jews from Elath; and the Syrians came to Elath, and lived there, to this day.

So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria, saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, who rise up against me.”
Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in Yahweh’s house, and in the treasures of the king’s house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria listened to him; and the king of Assyria went up against Damascus, and took it, and carried its people captive to Kir, and killed Rezin.
King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria, and saw the altar that was at Damascus; and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest a drawing of the altar and plans to build it.
Urijah the priest built an altar. According to all that king Ahaz had sent from Damascus, so Urijah the priest made it for the coming of king Ahaz from Damascus.
When the king had come from Damascus, the king saw the altar; and the king came near to the altar, and offered on it.
He burned his burnt offering and his meal offering, poured his drink offering, and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
The bronze altar, which was before Yahweh, he brought from the front of the house, from between his altar and Yahweh’s house, and put it on the north side of his altar.

King Ahaz commanded Urijah the priest, saying, “On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering, the evening meal offering, the king’s burnt offering, his meal offering, with the burnt offering of all the people of the land, their meal offering, and their drink offerings; and sprinkle on it all the blood of the burnt offering, and all the blood of the sacrifice; but the bronze altar will be for me to inquire by.”
Urijah the priest did so, according to all that king Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut off the panels of the bases, and removed the basin from off them, and took down the sea from off the bronze oxen that were under it, and put it on a pavement of stone.
He removed the covered way for the Sabbath that they had built in the house, and the king’s entry outside to Yahweh’s house, because of the king of Assyria.
Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz which he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Ahaz slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city, and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: A new king rises: Ahaz, son of Jotham. In the seventeenth year of Pekah's reign in the north, the southern throne shifts hands once more. These dates matter because they anchor us in history — they remind us that God sees every turn of power and every moment, even the ones we forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty years old, and already the writer marks him: 'He didn't do that which was right in Yahweh his God's eyes.' A young man with the royal seal, but without the heart that made David great. How quickly we learn to stray when no one teaches us to love what is true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Making his son pass through fire — the most grievous darkness, the very abominations God cast out before Israel. Ahaz chose to imitate the nations Israel was meant to displace. How near are we to our own moment when we forget what we were called to be?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High places, hills, and green trees — the familiar, pleasing altars of false worship. Every corner seemed to offer an easier path than obedience. We know the pull of it still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rezin and Pekah march against Ahaz with armies to break him. Yet Jerusalem held. Even when a king strays far from righteousness, God's hand keeps what He has chosen — not for our merit, but because His word stands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elath lost to Syria — the ancient Red Sea port, once Israel's gateway to trade and the wider world. The writer notes it lingers in his own time: 'to this day.' Some losses remain, witnesses to how far we fell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I am your servant and your son.' Ahaz bows to Assyria's king, calling himself vassal. Fear makes us say words we can't unsay. He sought rescue from a king of men rather than crying out to the King of heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver and gold from God's house — the very treasures meant to serve the Lord — sent as a bribe to Assyria. When we grow desperate, we spend the sacred things first. How do we reckon with that?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tiglath-Pileser moves swiftly, takes Damascus, carries its people to Kir, kills Rezin. Power shifts — but Ahaz has sold more than enemy weakness; he's mortgaged his people to a new master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz goes to Damascus to see the altar there — a pagan shrine in a conquered city — and becomes captivated by it. He sends designs back to Urijah the priest, commands it be built. This is the moment a king chooses to reshape the Lord's house in the image of the nations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Urijah the priest obeys. He builds the altar exactly as the king commanded, before the king even returns. How many times do we compromise something sacred simply because authority demands it? Urijah had a choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king comes from Damascus and sees his new altar. He approaches it, draws near, and offers on it. The pagan worship begins — not in some distant place, but in the very courts of God's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He offers burnt offering, meal offering, drink offering, sprinkles peace offerings' blood. All the forms of worship remain, but offered to the wrong God, in the wrong way. Ritual without obedience is a hollow thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old bronze altar — the one that had stood before Yahweh, between the house and His presence — is now shoved aside, moved to the north side to make room for the new pagan altar. What once held the center is displaced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz commands Urijah: all sacrifices — morning, evening, king's, people's — now burn on the new altar. But the bronze altar? 'For me to inquire by.' The king reserves it for his own divination, his private seeking. He has remade worship to suit his power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Urijah the priest did all of it. No resistance, no word of warning, no 'Thus says the Lord.' Sometimes the tragedy is not what the wicked do, but that the righteous go silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz cuts panels from the bases, removes the basin, takes down the bronze sea. The ornaments of God's house — each one part of its ordered beauty — are systematized stripped away. Piece by piece, the temple becomes unrecognizable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The covered way for the Sabbath — a shelter for the people to gather on God's rest day — is removed. The king's entry is cut back. All for 'the king of Assyria.' When we serve other powers, we unbuilding the shelter we made for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chronicler writes it down: 'the rest of the acts of Ahaz which he did.' Someone remembered, someone recorded. The full measure of a king's unfaithfulness lies in the annals, known to God. What we do is never truly hidden.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz slept with his fathers, buried in David's city — given a king's rest, though he had forsaken a king's God. Readers today hear an echo: even those who stray from faithfulness are still held by the promise made to David. The Lord's covenant stands, even when our hearts do not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
